      <description>Norwegian har teke kontakt med rundt 5000 kundar og bede dei sperre bankkorta sine etter at ein leverandør til nettsidene deira er utsett for datainnbrot, melder NTB.
Ein skadeleg kode blei lagt inn på nettsidene til Norwegian, som gjorde at kortdetaljar som blei brukt på nettsida kan ha vore synlege i ein kortare periode måndag.
Selskapet oppdaga datainnbrotet onsdag.
Hendinga er rapportert til Datatilsynet.

      <title>Israel med ny offensiv – tre drept</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/israel-med-ny-offensiv-_-tre-drept-1.18084431</link>
      <description>Israels hær sier den har innledet en operasjon i Hamas-kontrollerte områder i Gaza
Israel har innledet en militæroperasjon i det sentrale Gaza vest for den såkalte gule linjen, som har skilt Hamas-kontrollerte og israelsk-kontrollerte områder siden våpenhvilen trådte i kraft i fjor. Det opplyser militæret til AFP.
Vitner sier at israelske stridsvogner rullet inn på hovedveien Salahudeen, vest for den såkalte gule linjen som markerer grensen for de to tredjedelene av Gazastripen som fortsatt er under israelsk kontroll.
Den såkalte gule linjen ble etablert etter våpenhvilen i oktober 2025 og skiller israelskkontrollerte og palestinske soner i Gazastripen. Israelske styrker har gradvis flyttet den gule linjen og utvidet området under direkte militær kontroll i Gaza.</description>

Two MLAs from Vancouver Island are part of newly minted B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson’s cabinet.

Anna Kindy, MLA for North Island, was named Minister of State for Rural Development, while Cathie Ounsted, MLA for Saanich South, was named Minister for Local Government, Housing, Sports, and Culture.

Kindy was first elected in 2024 before being re-elected in the recent snap election, beating out the NDP’s Sara Lopez.

Ounsted is a political newcomer, being first elected in the October snap election.

]]> 1362860 Victoria art gallery selects architect for new space at Capital Iron redevelopment lands https://cheknews.ca/victoria-art-gallery-selects-architect-for-new-space-at-capital-iron-redevelopment-lands-1362838/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:31:16 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1362838

The Art Gallery of Greater Victoria has chosen a Vancouver-based architectural firm to design its new art gallery at the Capital Iron redevelopment area.

]]>

The Art Gallery of Greater Victoria (AGGV) has chosen a Vancouver-based architectural firm to design its new art gallery at the Capital Iron redevelopment area. 

The AGGV selected Michael Green Architecture (MGA) to design the new gallery, which it envisions as a space that will showcase more of its collection, celebrate Indigenous land and artists, and provide more opportunities for artists, educators and community connection.

The firm may be familiar to some, as it has taken on projects both internationally and locally, including in California, Spain, Sweden, Vancouver and Vancouver Island – including the new Royal BC Museum PARC Campus in Colwood, which is eyeing a 2027 opening.

“I am excited to work with the MGA team on the AGGV’s new building,” said Nancy Noble, director and CEO of the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria.

“They are rooted in this place and with their community-centered approach and commitment to sustainability, simplicity and durability, they are the right partner to help us realize our vision of engaging and inspiring through access to art,” she said.

An example of a building designed by MGA is shown below. The AGGV says no renderings of the new art gallery are available as the firm was just hired.

Victoria plans Capital Iron lands redevelopment

The new art gallery is destined for the City of Victoria’s new “Industry, Arts and Innovation District,” a large-scale redevelopment plan for the Rock Bay area north of downtown, which includes the well-known Capital Iron building.

The plan is nearing completion but has still not been fully adopted.

In January, Victoria council unanimously approved the third reading of bylaws necessary for the redevelopment, meaning only final adoption is still required.

The plan for the area – which includes 1824, 1900, 1907, 1908, 1924 and 2010 Store Street and 530 Chatham Street – is to create a mixed-use area with housing, commercial, industrial and public spaces called the Industry, Arts and Innovation District (IAID).

Some of the proposed buildings measure 14 storeys tall.

The plan has gone through years of revisions and rounds of public engagement. On Jan. 8, when the third reading was approved, there was a general sense of support for the redevelopment. Out of 39 public submissions heard and read at the meeting, only one letter was opposed.

Supporters from the public and at the council table said they favoured the added housing, retail space, and home for the arts with the new site of the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria, which would be part of the first phase of the redevelopment, which also includes construction of a public plaza.

However, concerns included the removal of industrial lands along the water, which are already limited in Victoria, and the overriding of some aspects of the newly completed Official Community Plan, which was passed by council in October 2025.

In the meantime, Michael Green Architecture says it’s excited to design the new Art Gallery of Greater Victoria.

“Economies shift and technologies change, but what lasts are the stories we tell, the creativity we foster, the culture we invest in, and the conversations we have,” said Michael Green, founder of Michael Green Architecture.

“Creating a new home for the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria is a wonderful opportunity for our city. We are grateful to the AGGV team for their vision and trust, and for their commitment to art, artists, and the community, with a space that will welcome everyone for generations to come,” he said.

– With files from CHEK’s Laura Brougham

The Pemberton Valley Dyking District says repair costs to its dikes after this month’s torrential rain and flooding will be “significant.”

The district manages 44 kilometres of dikes around the community in B.C.’s Sea to Sky region and says its infrastructure “took a fairly good beating” in the flooding that prompted an evacuation alert for all of Pemberton as rivers swelled with heavy rains.

The district’s update on social media says work is underway to assess the full extent of the damage from the first major storms of the season and once that’s done it must tally the cost of repairs. 

It says the immediate focus is repairs that “impact our ability to withstand another rain event or pose a public safety risk.”

The district says it’s planning to apply for provincial disaster financial assistance, but not all flood or emergency events qualify and it must plead its case. 

The series of storms earlier this month drenched southwestern B.C., where flood advisories spanned several regions, and four people died in as many days in rivers near Squamish, about 90 kilometres south of Pemberton.

The dyking district says it has done some emergency repairs on a culvert in Pemberton Creek and is in the process of removing log jams.

“For the larger repairs like Miller Weir and some yet to be quantified dike damage, we will have to see how this process moves as we go.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

Police in Vancouver say a man who pleaded guilty to child luring and possession of child abuse material after being caught in an undercover sting will go to jail for almost two years. 

Police say Gregory Ikert was arrested during a 2024 operation by the department’s Internet Child Exploitation Unit that targeted adults who sexually exploit children online. 

They say Ikert was arrested on Oct. 16, 2024, and a search of his home led to the seizure of electronic devices containing child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

The department says Ikert pleaded guilty on June 29, and was handed a sentence on Nov. 5 to two years less a day, ensuring that he will serve the time in provincial jail, instead of federal prison. 

It says Ikert is also required to register with the National Sex Offender Registry for 20 years and his DNA will be added to the National DNA Data Bank.

The court also imposed a five-year prohibition order, preventing him from going to public parks, public swimming areas, schoolgrounds and daycare centres unless under the supervision of a person which the court considers appropriate.

The department is also encouraging parents and caregivers to have conversations with children about online safety and report suspicious online activity involving minors to police.

Pichette, who spent more than 30 years working in finance, was grilled during the meeting over his relationship with Cohere and Inovia Capital.

A community favourite, festive competition has returned to Victoria in support of Habitat for Humanity.

The 18th annual Gingerbread Showcase launched at the Hotel Grand Pacific in downtown Victoria today, Nov. 20, featuring a range of locally-made gingerbread houses that feature remarkable levels of detail.

From now until Jan. 3, visitors can peruse the gingerbread creations for free from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily at the hotel at 463 Belleville Street. People can also vote on their favourite pieces of baked architecture in person in front of each gingerbread house or online.

Those donations go to Habitat for Humanity, which builds affordable houses in the community.

Nearly two decades on, the event sees an average of more than 20,000 visitors each year, ranging from school groups to locals to tourists.

This year, the theme for the Gingerbread Showcase is “Where Dreams Come True.” Bakers were asked to imagine what a safe home for dreaming may look like when assembling their creations. In the past, some creators said they spent dozens or even hundreds of hours creating their gingerbread houses, which must be made with all edible ingredients.

Thirty-four entries are on display this season, with a handful shown below.

Last year, the theme was “Homes for All,” and the Gingerbread Showcase raised nearly $120,000, setting a new record for the fundraiser.

Six winners are chosen at each showcase in the following categories:

  • Best First Impression
  • Best Use of Skill and Technique
  • Best Interpretation of the Theme
  • Most Creative and Original
  • Most Diverse Use of Ingredients
  • The People’s Choice Award

Last year, Geoff Cram from Old Town Bakery in Ladysmith took home the People’s Choice Award for his creation, An Oak River Christmas, with more than 4,700 votes.

“This is an event made by the community, for the community. Every gingerbread creation tells a tale, and when you visit, vote, and donate, you are helping write a much bigger chapter about building homes and hope right here in Greater Victoria,” said Carmen Rempel, CEO of Habitat Victoria.

The Hotel Grand Pacific also said it was happy to host the event again this year.

“The work Habitat for Humanity does to help local families build safe and affordable homes changes lives, and we are proud to support that mission,” said Hotel Grand Pacific general manager Uwe Walter.

“We look forward to welcoming guests to enjoy the creativity, community connection, and holiday magic that make this event so special.”

The post No changes to ‘core’ cadet programming after cancellation emails: defence minister appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

Defence Minister David McGuinty says there will be “no changes to core weekly programming” for the cadets after chapters received emails telling them to cancel weekend training, competitions and other activities through the end of March.

The internal emails, obtained by The Canadian Press, say the activities are being paused because of “the current fiscal environment.”

In a statement released Friday on social media, McGuinty said the program has “grown by 59 per cent in recent years” and its funding has been “significantly increased” while its leadership adjusts to changing priorities and needs.

“We have heard the concerns raised by cadets, families and communities across Canada about changes to planned cadet activities. We know how much this program means to young Canadians and the important role it plays in developing leadership, confidence and a commitment to service,” McGuinty said in his statement.

“I have asked officials to review the program’s funding and will ensure the cadet community is kept informed as that work progresses.”

The cadet program runs across Canada, with sea, army and air programs for youth aged 12 to 18. Members engage in military-style drills and take part in activities ranging from sailing to camping to glider flights.

A petition on the website Change.org is calling on the government to restore funding for the cancelled and suspended programming. The petition has received more than 31,000 signatures since it was launched on Tuesday.

The program’s budget is about $265 million this year, which includes a $27 million increase in funding announced in the spring.

Internal emails sent to cadet staff in Ontario and British Columbia say corps and squadron parade night training will continue, while several other activities are being cancelled or paused for the remainder of the fiscal year.

A Defence Department spokesperson said in an email the program has seen “increased interest and participation” that requires “additional consideration” of how funds are distributed across Canada.

The spokesperson added it is “too early” to determine the full extent of changes to cadet programming.

The cadet program had more than 61,000 participants in the last fiscal year, according to the Department of National Defence 2025-26 departmental results report.

A new war monument honouring the thousands of Canadians who fought in South Korea was unveiled in Langford on Thursday by the mayor of Gapyeong County, the City of Langford, Canadian veterans, the local Korean community, and community supporters.

The post Korean mayor, delegates help unveil war monument in Langford appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

A new war monument honouring the thousands of Canadians who fought in South Korea was unveiled in Langford on Thursday by the mayor of Gapyeong County, the City of Langford, Canadian veterans, the local Korean community, and community supporters.

The monument, called the Gapyeong Battle Victory Monument, was installed at Veterans Memorial Park, recognizing the 26,000 Canadians who fought for South Korea, including 516 who died.

According to the City of Langford, soldiers of the 2nd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry demonstrated “extraordinary courage and determination while defending their position against overwhelming enemy forces” during the Battle of Gapyeong in 1951.

Their courage helped repel an enemy breakthrough and “contributed significantly to the defence of South Korea,” says the city.

Two veterans of the battle, both 98-years-old, were at the ceremony and say the monument serves as an important reminder.

“There are others in Canada. It means a lot that we now have one on Vancouver Island,” said Korean War veteran Ted Adye. “We deal a lot with the Korean association here and they’re so kind to us.”

Adye hopes the monument in Langford will serve as a symbol for those who fought in a war that is sometimes overlooked in North America.

“Everyone remembers the Second World War and the First World War and all the big battles we fought, but they don’t remember a lot about Korea, and I think even Vietnam comes into it too. All of these are of great significance. It’s too bad we had to have them in the first place,” he said.

Seven people from Gapyeong County attended the unveiling, including Mayor Seo Tae-won. Local politicians, RCMP members, members of the Langford Legion, and a Songhees Nation Councillor were also in attendance.

“You have travelled a long way to be here today, and I am deeply honoured that you chose Langford as the place where this memorial stone, shipped all the way from Gapyeong, will stand as a lasting connection to our shared history,” said Langford Mayor Stew Young at the ceremony.

]]> 1362804 Historic guns locked away as RCMP centre set to become next national museum https://cheknews.ca/historic-guns-locked-away-as-rcmp-centre-set-to-become-next-national-museum-1362801/ Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:40:00 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1362801

At the RCMP Heritage Centre in Regina, which is set to become Canada's next national museum, one display case is glaringly empty, "Weapons of the Plains." Vintage RCMP carbines and revolvers used over 140 years ago are no longer on display.

The post Historic guns locked away as RCMP centre set to become next national museum appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

At the RCMP Heritage Centre in Regina, which is set to become Canada’s next national museum, one display case is glaringly empty.

The large wood and glass cabinet is supposed to show “Weapons of the Plains,” but the only things inside are wall labels and empty hooks. 

Vintage RCMP carbines and revolvers used over 140 years ago are no longer on display. And gone are the antique rifles used by Prairie settlers and Indigenous people. 

All other displays have had guns removed too. 

The centre, known for its vintage memorabilia and tales of true crime, says the weapons have been locked away.

The federal government announced earlier this month that it plans to designate the centre a national museum. Ottawa’s budget says the centre is to receive $3 million in annual funding for national designation.

Sam Karikas, the centre’s CEO, said the guns were removed a year ago to comply with provincial firearms regulations. The RCMP owns the weapons and provided them on loan.

“In order to have them on display, we would need to alter the firearms, which the RCMP doesn’t want to do,” Karikas said in an email.

“We’re currently working on solutions and are hoping to have printed replicas introduced early in the new year.”

One firearm removed from the museum is the rifle of Sam Steele, a prominent Mountie who helped bring law to the West in the 1870s. 

Also gone is the RCMP’s centennial rifle, made in 1973 to mark the force’s 100th anniversary.

A 1920s machine gun, gas guns from the 1960s and a harpoon gun used in a former northern detachment were placed in storage. Even a pistol from a modern-day duty belt was taken out of the museum.

Still on display are some swords, batons, homemade weapons used in the Regina riot of 1935, and a bow and arrow from 1876. There’s also memorabilia from Métis leader Louis Riel, including his knife, crucifix, Bible and revolver holster. 

RCMP said their historical collections unit removed the guns to be in compliance with a decision made by both the Saskatchewan Firearms Office and federal firearms legislation. 

“The firearms in the collection are stored in an RCMP secured vault for storage,” Mounties said in an emailed statement.

In response to questions to the firearms office, a spokesperson from Premier Scott Moe’s office said Saskatchewan’s regulations align with Ottawa’s and don’t impose additional requirements. 

“It is more likely that the RCMP Heritage Centre’s issue arises from requirements or standards established by the Museum Association of Saskatchewan, rather than from any provincial government body, provincial legislation or regulations,” the spokesperson said in an email.

Emma Morris, executive director of the museum association, said it doesn’t regulate firearms but provides recommendations.

Federal regulations state museums with guns on display must have a valid firearms business licence and all staff must have a valid possession and acquisition licence. 

Regulations also require a gun on display to be secured by a metal bar and with a chain or metal cable that passes through the trigger guard. A firearm should also be rendered inoperable by a secure locking device.

Morris added that the regulations don’t say whether a firearm should be deactivated, which requires permanent alteration making it inoperable.

“We really don’t want somebody to steal a firearm and use it to hold up a gas station or a school and cause a very real threat in their community,” she said. “There is that liability risk.”

The association previously flagged a case where nine handguns were stolen from a Saskatchewan museum.

Morris said she has no details on when or where that theft happened, as it was before her time as executive director.

Other museums in the province currently display guns, including the Saskatoon Police Museum.

A spokesperson with the Saskatoon force said those firearms were rendered inoperable before being placed in locked cabinets.

Meanwhile, Karikas said she’s looking forward to the centre becoming a national museum. It would be the country’s 10th national museum and the second in Western Canada. 

The federal funding would also help it enhance services, she said.

“We have a lot of room to grow in the stories that we’re telling, particularly around more of the complex nature of what happens at the time of colonialization,” Karikas said. 

“We would not be at 160 years of Confederation were it not for the establishment of the North West Mounted Police. With that, of course, comes a whole lot of complexity and colonial stories of what that looks like.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

Vancouver Island blues-rock guitarist Garret T. Willie is used to collecting stories from the road, but one of his most frightening has nothing to do with touring or playing music. After weeks of recovery, the 26-year-old is finally ready to share the story of a motorcycle ride that nearly cost him his life.

It happened Sept. 25, when Willie was visiting family in Campbell River. With a new motorcycle and some good weather in the forecast, he saw an opportunity to enjoy the ride before heading back home to Courtenay.

“I’d just got this nice motorcycle and it was supposed to be nice that weekend so I just wanted to go up there and enjoy the weather and all that,” Willie said.

It’s been a busy couple of years for Willie, who has taken his blues-rock sound well beyond Vancouver Island. His debut album, Same Pain, cracked the Top 20 on blues charts in both the U.K. and U.S., earned him two Western Canadian Music Award nominations and landed him opening slots for the likes of John Fogerty, Joe Bonamassa and Kenny Wayne Shepherd.

His band had recently completed its first tours of the United Kingdom and the United States, with another European tour planned for next year, so the September weekend was a chance to unwind before getting back to a busy schedule.

That night, Willie decided to make the trip home by motorcycle, figuring the Inland Island Highway (Hwy 19) would be the quicker route.

“My thinking at the time was, ‘It’ll be quicker taking the Inland’. I was taking the Inland from Courtenay to Campbell,” he said.

It was dark when he set off, and not long into the ride, everything changed.

“About 20 minutes into my ride a black bear jumped the centre median and before I could do anything I went right into him,” Willie recalled.

Travelling at approximately 110 km/h, he collided head-on with the bear, sending him over his handlebars and onto the pavement.

“I hit him, I went over my handlebars and was knocked unconscious.”

When Willie eventually regained consciousness, he found himself in the ditch, surrounded by the aftermath of the collision.

“I looked around at my surroundings. I saw my bike in the ditch still running with the headlight on and further up in the ditch was the bear.”

The bear died, and Willie suffered devastating injuries, including a compound fracture of the tibia and fibula on his right leg, a broken right hand and a concussion, along with scrapes and bruises across his face and body.

He managed to call family, but his phone died within seconds, leaving him to try to get help from passing motorists.

“About two or three cars went by, and didn’t stop,” he said.

With his injuries making it difficult to move, Willie eventually pulled himself toward the centre median, hoping someone would see him and stop. More cars passed despite him desperately signalling for help. Before long there was no traffic passing at all.

He spent roughly an hour sitting alone in the darkness, bleeding and badly injured, needing urgent care. Having no idea when help might arrive, the isolation and fear became so overwhelming that he began to lose hope.

“My leg was bleeding badly, and I thought if I was going to bleed out here I might as well … I thought I was going to cut my wrists,” he said.

Thankfully, headlights appeared in the distance, and this time the approaching vehicle was an RCMP cruiser.

“I’ve never been so glad to see them in my life,” Willie said.

He was taken to hospital in Campbell River, where doctors faced the difficult prospect of dealing with his badly shattered leg.

“They said they might take my leg because of how badly broken it was,” he recalled.

Fortunately, surgeons were able to save it, and about a month and a half after the collision, Willie is back home in Courtenay, making progress in his recovery.

The pins have since come out of his broken picking hand, and he’s already managed to get back to the instrument that has defined so much of his life.

“I played guitar the other day, which was nice,” he said.

For a musician whose livelihood depends on his hands, even that small accomplishment represents a significant step forward. Willie had been building momentum with his band following its first international tours, but getting back on stage and returning to the road will have to wait until he’s further along in his recovery.

For now, his ambitions are much simpler.

“I just want to walk,” he said.

After an experience that could have ended very differently, Willie says he’s grateful for the opportunity to keep moving forward, even if it’s one small step at a time.

“Glad to have a second shot at life,” he said.
